So either the line is refused for heap enemies too, or the last link frees an arena block through the built-in manager. The `owns this` end and a thread_shared owner made in code compiled once have the same gap.

Neither design text nor ALC-1 (p09-memory.md:184-213) says where `copy of` a value made in an instance takes its memory, and Clone is field-wise with no manager (p14-comptime.md:127). The design's facet 4 ('what its methods make for those fields ... in the instance the value is made in') invites the source's instance. Then both tasks call `level.allocate`, while the design states 'a read never touches the manager'. The outcome is either a race on the cursor or E7007, which contradicts the design's own claim. The program is undecided.

THR-21 p11-concurrency.md:415 says 'Each task's accumulator has the place's type', which here is `Array[int] using Arena` with no instance. LT-46 p07:688-689 lets a sharedref mut target change on two threads 'by a reduction from scoped tasks', while the design's ALC-6 3 counts growth as a change of the instance (two tasks: E7007). The design decides neither reading.

The rules refuse the push. Design rule (3): 'a value's growth and its end call its instance', and spec_text ALC-6 3: 'its growth and end count as changes of the instance'. Design ARN-6: 'Allocating from the parent ... while the scope lives is E3096'. Spec LT-4 p07:621-623: 'each value's growth and end change the instance through it'. causes.cause: Which manager a value comes from (its kind, and its instance) is part of what the value is. The first design ties the kind only to a listed set of keeping places. Every other name may take a value without knowing its kind: a result, an element, a plain or ref mut parameter, `this`, a kept view, a `dyn`, a function value. A body compiled once then grows, gives back, links, owns or counts the value with the wrong manager. Elsewhere it demands a `using` the caller already knows.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 53 (JOB.md:420-434), with 54 and 87: a fact worked out from a body is kept with the function and checked at each call. Here the fact is which parameters' kind or instance the body depends on, and what it does to them. Verdict 88 (JOB.md:661-667): the compiler makes a copy of the function where the body depends on the caller. Verdict 128 (JOB.md:1040): a parameter holds what its callers pass. LT-1 p07:544-555 and verdict 151: a dyn or virtual call is decided by the code of each kind that may reach it, and a kind known only while running is refused unless `runtime` is written (verdict 152, LT-48 p07:704-713). EFF-24 p10:90-103 is the summary that carries the fact.
causes.why: For every program of this cause the compiler can work out the kind and the instance where the call is made: from the caller's value, or from every value the program can put behind a dyn or a function value (EFF-2, verdict 129). Nothing runs for it: a copy per kind where the body depends on the kind, a check at the call otherwise. A kind known only while running is already refused by LT-1's rule. One point must still be said plainly to the owner as part of the rule (D.5), not as an ODR: verdict 19's 'Without using, the built-in memory manager' would then govern only places that keep a value, and a parameter takes its caller's kind. Both designs list 19 as kept as given.

causes.cause: One keeping place (a weakref field, a class-object owner place) may be given values from managers of different kinds over its life. Only the value's own block knows which manager takes it back.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 24 (JOB.md:216-221), with verdict 19's `mesh: shares Mesh using LevelArena` (JOB.md:190-191): an owner field says the kind, so it holds values of one kind. No verdict covers a weakref field, or a list of class objects meant to hold a heap player beside arena enemies.
causes.why: The program: `cam.target = weakref boss` with `boss` made `using level`, then `cam.target = weakref player` from the built-in manager (H16). Which manager takes the block back at the link's last end is known only while the program runs, so the compiler cannot work it out. Three answers remain. (a) The field names the kind, as verdict 24 does for owner fields; the camera then cannot follow both. (b) The block records its kind and the last end gives it back through that record: one indirect call per last give-back, plus a type index per kind (H61), to measure. (c) A refusal. The first design and method 1's repair chose differently, and extending verdict 24 to links would widen it.

causes.cause: What giving memory back ends, and while what it is refused. The first design ties both to one merged notion of 'reaches' (holds an address, or will call later) over a value's whole life. It lists the instance changes allowed under live values, and states its own ends as the only ends. Instead, a give-back should be a reshape of the memory it gives back. It then ends exactly what holds into that memory at that point (a view until its last use, an owner or a link until its end touches the block), beside every other end.
causes.existing_answer: The view rules already state this for every reshape. BRW-2 p07:280-282: a view lives until its last use. BRW-17 p07:431-436: a view ends at any reshape made through any name that may reach it, and two paths of one type, one through a link, may reach one object. BCK-4 p18:185-188. ARN-1 p09:102-103: views point into the arena's memory, not its cursor. Across calls, LT-47 p07:694-701 with the EFF-24 summary and verdict 53 carry what a callee leaves in a ref mut place and whether a result holds a block. RC-3 p08:148-151: an end that moves no drop may move. For parts the compiler cannot follow, LT-45 p07:658-659: a list of views keeps what it points into for its whole life, a limitation already stated.
causes.why: These rules decide every program of this cause when compiling, applied to the instance's memory as to any place. Where the compiler cannot tell which elements still hold into the memory (a clear by computed index), the refusal is the one a list of views already gets (LT-45): an understandable limitation, stated clearly (principle 7). No word and no run-time check is needed.

causes.cause: Where a value takes its memory when its line names no instance: a copy, a clone, a sum or conversion, a value made inside a callee, a constructor argument or list element for a part tied to the whole value's manager, and a task's accumulator. The first design names only field defaults and the fields a type's methods make.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 24 (JOB.md:216-221): the line that makes the value says which instance. Verdict 19 and ALC-1 p09:188-189: without `using`, the built-in manager. ALC-1 p09:202-203 and TYP-46 p04:444-446: what a value holds comes from where its own types say. GRM-43 p03:435-438. The first design's own facet-4 sentence: a `using A` part takes the whole value's instance. Together these settle a copy, a sum and an accumulator (built-in unless the line names an instance; the join grows the place on the parent's thread), and the parts and arguments of a value made `using m` (made in m).
causes.why: One part stays open: a value made inside a body that has no line to name the caller's instance, for a place whose type fixes a kind with several instances. Examples: `[T: needs Clone] fn dup(x: T) -> T: return copy of x` given a `Token using Arena` while two Arenas live; std's `to_key` making a `String using Arena` key for `counts[w] = 1`; a clone that delegates to a helper; a task's accumulator for arena-kind elements. The compiler cannot work out which instance is meant. Three answers remain. (a) A written word: new syntax naming the instance at the call, such as `dup(t) using level` (checklist 12). (b) An unwritten default: the source's or the container's instance, as Rust does, which verdict 24 and principle 2's 'no silent decision' argue against. (c) A refusal: E2020 with help.

causes.cause: Verdict 107 drops the instance word by the kind of manager, but whether a value can do without the word depends on the value. causes.cause: The first design derives a value's thread markers from the hidden instance link as if every name held the link and every operation used it, and it decides the link from allocate, deallocate and reallocate together. In fact the link is used only by the operations that call the manager (growth, end, a making for parts), only through names that may run them, and only through the methods those operations reach.
causes.existing_answer: THR-8 and THR-9 (p11:43-68) define Send by what a holder on another thread may do, and ThreadShared by reading. Verdict 164 (JOB.md:1251) covers a link through which holders change a target. Verdict 166 (JOB.md:1255) treats a task's operation on one-thread state as the route, per operation. EXC-15 p08:268-271 and verdict 86: what a method changes is inferred from its body. Verdict 107 b: an empty deallocate is checked when compiling. Verdict 19: `using Global` names the built-in manager. Verdict 101 fix 2 (JOB.md:799-800): a hand-over the compiler sees moves the home count, decided when compiling.
causes.why: Which operations a name may run on another thread, and which manager methods those operations reach, is known when compiling. So every program of this cause is decided with no word and no run-time cost. The header layout for values never counted at home (H24) is a cost to state and measure, not a language decision.

causes.cause: The rule relies on two facts about a program's own manager that the compiler cannot check from its body, and ALC-2's promise states neither. First, no block still given out is freed except by deallocate, reallocate, the instance's end, or a change made through a name that may change the instance (the only changes ALC-5 sees). Second, the manager's methods keep their guarantees when called from several threads at once.
causes.existing_answer: ALC-2 p09:228-230 and TYP-43: implementing Allocator is an unsafe promise, the place where such facts are vouched. THR-8 p11:54-58: a fact about threads that the compiler cannot see is vouched with `unsafe extend ... implements Send:`. THR-7 p11:131-133: two Atomic operations are two steps. P04's principle: safe code relies only on what is checked or vouched. Rust's Allocator and GlobalAlloc contract: memory stays valid until deallocated, and Sync covers calls from several threads.
causes.why: Both facts belong in the implementer's existing promise. No program of this cause needs a run-time check, and safe code is unchanged.

[THR-19] (p11-concurrency.md:267-284) misses the same case for a written `with POOL_LOCK:` in that loop. Once THR-19 sees a lock held across a yield, P05 gets the answer for free (a run-time held-lock count under cause P05-C1 would catch it too).

The first design's RC-4 point 6 (P05.json:7) says the taker 'takes that queue (one compare-and-exchange), adds the value's home count into its away count, ends the value when the sum is zero, and gives the queue back'. RC-8 says 'Ending a value runs its drop'. So ~Conn() runs while the taker holds main's queue. Ending its field `pool`, an owner made on main and counted in the Pool's home count, then needs main's queue again. The text never says what a putter that finds the queue taken does, but a thread leaving rest 'waits while another thread holds it'. Cost item 7 (P05.json:97) gives a third order ('take ... give it back, then the merge'), under which the merge races with main leaving rest on the plain home count ([RC-4] point 1, p08-classes.md:159-162: only the making thread reads both). Cause P05-C3.

By [FFI-52] (p16-ffi.md:451-458), `bus_dispatch()` may run the kept `on_event`. The first design sets the thread's mark around a foreign call that may run kept callbacks only when the call is made 'while this thread holds a lock, or ... from a function under such a contract' (RC-4 point 3, P05.json:7). Main calls `bus_dispatch()` holding nothing. So `on_event`'s back edge, judged from its own code, is clear, and ~Sub() calls `bus_unsubscribe` inside C's dispatch, where C holds the bus mutex. The function's @safety forbids exactly that: undefined behaviour at a site the compiler picked and no `# SAFETY:` note can cover. Cause P05-C1.

The first design's RT-8 change says 'Entering rest is a release: one exchange of the thread's queue word', after 'It first empties its queue' (RC-4 point 6, P05.json:7). A push that lands between the two is either overwritten, so Texture 1 is never ended (J7-02's leak again), or handed back to a thread whose word already says 'at rest' while takers merge the same plain home count ([RC-4] point 1, p08-classes.md:159-162). Under [RC-4] point 4 (p08-classes.md:173-178), a store into a lock-guarded container that other threads can reach 'first adds its own count of the value into the away count', which writes the home count. The first design's FFI-22 change leaves an outermost call at rest unless its code 'may make, end or open an owner'. `on_flush` only pops an owner and pushes it into `SAVED`, so it runs at rest while it writes the home count. A worker's end can then take over and merge the same field: a data race on a plain count. The COST-3 change in the same design says 'may touch a thread_shared count', so the two texts disagree. Cause P05-C3.

The first design's clear test looks only at locks this thread holds, walks, views and contracts (RC-8 point 2, P05.json:7). A bounded `send` blocks while the channel is full ([THR-15], p11-concurrency.md:337-339), and it is not even in the Block row (p10-effects.md:14). Main's inner back edge is clear: ~Conn(1) fills the one slot, then ~Conn(2) waits for a receiver that is main itself. [DRP-4] (p07-ownership.md:849-850) only says a drop SHOULD NOT block. Run on the worker, where the last owner ended (C++, Rust), the program finishes. Cause P05-C2.

The first design places a point 'before every call that may block the thread' (RC-4 point 3, P05.json:7). That point is clear before `tx.send`, since main holds nothing. ~Conn() runs there and waits for `pool.lock`, which the worker holds while it waits in `for id in rx` for main's next send. [THR-19] (p11-concurrency.md:267-284) refuses joins, scope ends and lock-taking calls inside a lock, but not a receive, so both sides compile, and in this interleaving both wait for ever. The design's misuse text calls this C++'s behaviour too, but in C++ the destructor runs on the worker at `b.conns.clear()`, before it locks. Cause P05-C2.

Under [PAR-4] (p11-concurrency.md:485-487), 'when they are full the calling thread runs the chunk itself'. So ~Conn() waits there for the lock W itself holds. Stealing other jobs while waiting is not stated in the specification; the PAR-4 path is enough. Cause P05-C1.

The first design's rest states (RC-4 point 6, P05.json:7) are: ended, returned from the outermost call to C, waiting for work in the job system, or asleep 'inside a blocking call made at a clear point' on the runtime's sleeping path. A blocking foreign call (`net_accept`) is none of them. So Conns queued to main wait for the next client, or for ever inside a loop that lives in C. That breaks P05's own bound, 'before the thread waits idle, leaves Ember for C' (phase1-groups.json:158). Cause P05-C3.

RC-4 point 6 says only 'ends the value when the sum is zero', in the first design and in the repair alike (P05.json:7 and 150). With main's own owner still live, the sum is 1, and neither text says that the home count is then zeroed and the value marked handed over. The contradiction is between two pieces of the repair's text: 'rest needs no clear point ... A value it cannot end there stays queued' and the 'compare-and-exchange ... from empty to at rest' (P05.json:150). The first design rests only in a blocking call made at a clear point (P05.json:7), where the thread can empty its queue. So `wait_turn`, inside @noalloc, does not rest, and the Texture is ended at the first clear point after it returns.

The first design says 'A thread leaving rest takes its queue back (one compare-and-exchange), and waits while another thread holds it' (RC-4 point 6, P05.json:7). A taker holds the queue across the merge and, by the literal order, across the drop. So `on_midi`'s entry waits on the drain thread's progress: a priority inversion that is in no line and no effect. With SCHED_FIFO on one core it may never end (to verify). Cause P05-C3.

So the allocating Grain drops run after `mix`'s last line, yet still inside the C driver's call to a @noalloc export (FFI-22 change: 'empties its queue'). A job's captured state lives in its queue slot ([JOB-1], p11-concurrency.md:517-518), and the job system ends it after the function returns, at no line of the program. The first design's point 1 checks ends 'where the source puts them', and point 2 lists only queued values and a reload's reclaim. So this end has no stated point. causes.cause: A placed end runs user code (a drop, and the queue's own merge) at a point the program's text does not show. So whether it may run there depends on everything that holds on that thread at that moment: the locks, views, walks and contracts of every frame below, what C holds below a callback, the runtime's own work, a reload in progress, the emptying itself, and drops that another package or a later image may supply. The first design judges each point from one function's own code. It carries the callers' state down only for locks and contracts, and only along a list of call kinds (a copy for direct calls, a mark around indirect and foreign calls made in a lock or a contract).
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 53 (JOB.md:420-434): a fact worked out from a body is kept with the function, in the interface file across a package's edge, and checked at each call. Here the fact is 'this function may run a placed end', checked against the caller's held locks, live views and walks, and contracts. Verdict 88 (JOB.md:661-679): a copy of the function for that call. Verdict 31 (JOB.md:267-278) and [FFI-52] (p16-ffi.md:451-462): a foreign call counts as possibly running whatever C can reach, which is the default for code the compiler cannot see. [HR-44] (p20-annex-b.md:54-72) and [EFF-4] (p10-effects.md:52-64): the facts that code was checked against are compared at a reload and recorded at a package's edge. The first design already uses verdict 88's copy for locks and contracts; this cause needs the same for every context, the end's own Sync work included.
causes.why: The compiler can work the context out without a word, without a refusal and without a run-time check of the program. Under verdicts 53 and 88, each call is compiled against what its caller holds: a copy without points, or one thread-local mark for a call the compiler cannot follow. Verdict 31's default covers C frames: no placed end runs while a foreign call that may call back is below, and those values wait until the thread leaves C or rests (P05-C3). HR-44 and EFF-4 carry the facts across reloads and package edges. Nothing is refused or written; the mark costs one thread-local add and one subtract, only around calls the compiler cannot follow (to measure). H1's lock held across a yield is THR-19's question (elsewhere), which this cause then inherits.

causes.cause: A queued drop runs on the thread that made the value, not where its last owner ended, so every wait inside the drop moves to that thread. Whether the wait can be released without that thread's own later progress is a run-time relation: a bounded channel only it drains, a lock held by a thread that waits for it, a flag it sets after its loop, a pipe it reads. The clear-point test sees only what the thread holds at the point.
causes.existing_answer: None decides it. The nearest tool is verdict 101's fix 2 (JOB.md:799-800, 'a hand-over the compiler sees moves A into B at that moment'). Applied where a value of such a type is made, it lets the thread that ends the last owner run the drop, as C++ and Rust do. That is method 1's point 2, which narrows verdict 101, needs a 'may be queued' scope (H42) and needs an answer at a package's edge (H28, H48). [DRP-4] (p07-ownership.md:849-850), 'A drop SHOULD NOT block', states the limitation without deciding it.
causes.why: Take H6, a program that is correct in C++ and Rust. Left in the queue, it hangs. Run where its last owner ends, its type needs atomic counts from the start: verdict 101's 25% is lost for that type, and 101's 'that thread deletes it' is narrowed. A runtime drop thread contradicts verdict 101 and adds a hidden thread. A refusal refuses a correct program. Each option gives up one of the owner's requirements. The compiler can tell that a drop may wait (Block and Lock, once P14 makes Block cover a bounded send and a blocking write), but not that a hand-built spin is a wait (H47), and never whether the release depends on the making thread. So only a choice of cost, a refusal or a stated limitation remains, and verdict 101's text changes with any of them.

causes.cause: Only the making thread may read a value's home count (verdict 101). So a value queued to a thread that is not running Ember code (idle in the job system, back in C, inside a blocking or foreign call, or ended) is ended either when that thread runs again or by another thread that takes over the home count while the maker is guaranteed not to touch it. The first design adds that takeover as a new concurrent protocol but never states it as one ordered whole: entering rest, the take, the non-zero sum, the give-back, leaving rest without waiting, which code touches a home count, and how long a thread's record lives. It also lists only some of the states in which a thread stops running Ember code.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 101 (JOB.md:793-796), 'or the other thread deletes it at once if the making thread has ended' ([RC-4] point 3, p08-classes.md:171-172), is the takeover for the one state it names. Verdict 101's shortcut, 'A merged object's −1 is one locked add' (JOB.md:803), answers the non-zero sum (H29, H51). [HR-42] and [HR-42a] (p20-annex-b.md:73-78) give an existing per-thread 'inside Ember code' counter, entered with acquire and left with release: the publication a rest state needs, shared with reload. Nothing answers widening 'has ended' to the other states.
causes.why: The compiler cannot know when a thread will be idle or inside C. The J7-02 worker never ends and reaches no point, so under verdict 101's letter ('has ended') a Texture it made is held for the life of the process. Only run-time means remain: another thread takes over while the maker is at rest, or the maker is woken for each value. Both change verdict 101's text. The first design itself marks 'has ended' becoming 'is at rest' as needing the owner's yes, and H26 shows it is two questions: idle workers, threads back in C and ended threads, then any thread asleep in a blocking call. The protocol details (H2, H4, H5, H18, H29, H31) are the lead's to state once the owner answers.

causes.cause: The rule fixes by a list the places where ends the program does not write may run: every back edge, the compensating ends of three kinds of region, polls for a reload's reclaim, the outermost return, and the source lines of point 1. It does not state the property each place must have: a bounded amount of work between points, only on a thread that may have values queued; a point after every region that kept one out; and one stated point for every unwritten end, including the runtime's end of a function value and a reload's removed fields. Every place left off the list holds a value too long, costs a test where none is needed, or runs an end at a point nobody stated.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 101 (JOB.md:794-795) says the check point is 'placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends', which leaves placement wholly to the compiler. The back-edge list in [RC-4] point 3 is a lead choice the owner may overturn (decisions.md section 6, line 127). The first design's own compiler_does 1 already works out, per thread entry, which types may be queued.
causes.why: The compiler can place points by the property without a word or a refusal. It places none where no value can be queued, tests a loop whose trip count is known once every N rounds (strip-mined, so the loop still vectorises), polls at a recursive call group's entry, and puts a point after every region that kept one out. Every unwritten end then has one stated point: the end of a function value the runtime runs is the end of its body block on that thread, and a reload's removed fields are ended at the first clear point of the thread that owns them. The costs (N, the effect on vectorisation) are to measure.

causes.cause: The E7018 fix for a local made inside a lock, whose drop takes that lock, offers a line that does not compile: a block's local ends with its block ([DRP-2]), and its arguments may need the lock.
causes.existing_answer: Verdict 73 and checklist item 9 (OWNER-DIRECTION.md:158-159 and 249): every message gives a line that compiles; [DIA-28]. The wording is the lead's.
causes.why: It is message wording, not a language decision (checklist 19). The lead gives a line that compiles, for example `c: Option[Conn] = None` above the `with` line.

problems.rule: D4 (a choice made but missing from decisions_taken, and against the order of the owner's parameters)
problems.where: spec_text `[RC-4]` point 6: "sleeps in a blocking call (a foreign one too, when its `@ffi(effects=[…])` names `Block`)"; other_cases H15: "Had the effects been left out, main would not rest, and the buffers would be freed at main's next crossing between Ember and C (a callback's entry or return) or when the loop returns"; open_risks: "This rule reads only written effects for rest."
problems.why: Whether a foreign call with no stated effects rests the thread is a real choice that the design made but did not record. H44 offered two answers: rest only when the written effects name `Block`, or keep the stated default and give rest a fast path of plain stores, with the rare taker paying a process-wide barrier (the HotSpot/.NET way, which needs no word). The design took the first. It moves the second into open_risks as a cost variant. The choice is not in decisions_taken, and it has no options as code and outcome, no owner_short and no D4 ordering. It also departs from the nearest stated rule without saying so: `[FFI-10]` (p16-ffi.md:75) says a foreign function has "every effect when none are stated", and that includes `Block`. So the H15 outcome contradicts the spec as written. The choice also cuts against D4's order and decision 2's own reason. A thread inside an undeclared C event loop (H15) holds its queued memory for the whole run unless the programmer writes `@ffi(effects=[Block])`. That is the unbounded holding decision 2 was chosen to end ("B, C and D each leave a kind of thread out"), and here the fix is a word the programmer must write, while the other H44 option needs none (C3, principle 1).

problems.rule: An entry of rules_checked (and of verdicts) that is untrue
problems.where: rules_checked E: "15: a foreign call rests only when its written effects name `Block` (verdict 132)."; verdicts, 132: "kept ... An unwritten effect set does not fall back to a guess that would wrap every C call in two atomics (H44)."
problems.why: Verdict 132 (JOB.md:1052-1055) says that an unwritten `@ffi(const)` takes the language's stated default ("changes its object") and not a fact inferred from a body the reader cannot see. Here the stated default for unwritten effects is `[FFI-10]`'s "every effect". That is a written rule, not a guess. Applied here, verdict 132 points to the stated default, not to "rest only on written Block". So checklist item 15 and verdict 132 do not give this behaviour. The entry passes off an unrecorded choice, made for cost, as an application of a verdict.
